expertInsight: System Architect is earned by holding four credentials: Platform Developer I, Integration Architect, Identity and Access Management Architect, and Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect. There is no extra System Architect exam. Once the fourth one is passed, the credential is added to your profile. Platform Developer I is the only one that also counts toward Application Architect, so the other three are new work even if you already hold Application Architect.

whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the System Architect exam for?

personas.label: Enterprise Architects
personas.description: You design how Salesforce fits with the rest of the company's systems, logins and release process.

personas.label: Integration Specialists
personas.description: You already work on APIs and middleware and want the wider architect credential that covers identity and deployment too.

personas.label: IT Leaders
personas.description: You want your team to have a recognised path toward Technical Architect (CTA).

examDifficulty.heading: Is the System Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: System Architect has no exam of its own. You earn it automatically once you hold four credentials: Platform Developer I, Platform Integration Architect, Platform Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, and Identity and Access Management Architect. The hard part is the breadth, since those exams cover integration, logins and release management.
bullets: No separate exam. The credential is granted when you hold all four required certifications.
Four exams to pass. Platform Developer I, Integration Architect, Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, and Identity and Access Management Architect.
Wide scope. Together they cover integration patterns, OAuth and single sign-on, sandbox strategy and release management.
Check each exam's guide. Each of the four exams has its own format, pass mark and fee, listed in its official exam guide.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Most people take Platform Developer I first, then the three architect exams in whatever order matches their work. Plan each one on its own and use that exam's practice tests.

examFormat.heading: System Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: There is no System Architect exam to book. Here is how the credential works:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Each of the four exams uses short business scenarios. You read a requirement, such as a new partner portal login or a nightly data sync, and choose the best design.
bestWayToPass: Start with Platform Developer I: It gives you the Apex and data model basics that the architect exams assume.
Take Integration Architect next if you work with APIs: It covers patterns, APIs and error handling. See the Integration Architect guide.
Then Identity and Access Management: Learn SAML, OAuth flows, My Domain and how users are provisioned.
Finish with Development Lifecycle and Deployment: Sandboxes, source control, testing and release planning.

certificationCard.description: System Architect is earned, not tested. You get it when you hold Platform Developer I, Integration Architect, Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect, and Identity and Access Management Architect.

keyConcepts.h2: System Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns: Choosing the Right Approach
blocks.body: From the Integration Architect exam. Pick the pattern from three facts in the scenario: does a user wait for an answer, how much data is there, and which system starts the exchange. **Request and Reply** when the user waits. **Fire and Forget** with Platform Events or outbound messages when nobody waits. **Batch** with Bulk API for large scheduled loads. **Data Virtualization** with Salesforce Connect when data should stay in the other system. Callout limits matter: 100 callouts per transaction and 120 seconds in total.

blocks.heading: Authentication Patterns: OAuth 2.0 Flows
blocks.body: From the Identity and Access Management exam. **Web server flow** when a person logs in through a browser and the app can keep a secret on its server. **User-agent flow** for apps that run in a browser or on a phone. **JWT bearer flow** for server-to-server access with no person present. **Device flow** for things like TVs or command-line tools with no proper keyboard. **Refresh tokens** let an app get a new access token without asking the user again. Each flow is set up in a Connected App or External Client App; which also controls scopes and policies.

blocks.heading: API-Led Connectivity and Middleware (MuleSoft)
blocks.body: Once several systems share data, direct point-to-point links become hard to manage. Middleware sits in the middle. MuleSoft's model has three layers. **System APIs** talk to back-end systems. **Process APIs** combine data and apply business rules. **Experience APIs** shape data for one app or channel. This lets teams reuse the same APIs instead of building new connections for every project. In Salesforce, **Named Credentials** hold endpoints and login details so code never contains secrets.

blocks.heading: Sandbox Strategy and Release Management
blocks.body: From the Development Lifecycle and Deployment exam. Developer sandboxes for each developer, Partial Copy for QA, Full for performance and final user testing. Keep source in Git and deploy with the Salesforce CLI or DevOps Center. Production deployments with Apex need 75% test coverage. Validate early and quick deploy within 10 days. There is no rollback button, so keep the last good version in source control and use feature flags.

blocks.heading: Identity, SSO, and My Domain
blocks.body: Single sign-on lets users log in to Salesforce with the company's existing identity provider. With **SAML**, the company's provider (such as Okta or Entra ID) is the identity provider and Salesforce is the service provider. Salesforce can also be the identity provider for other apps. **My Domain** gives your org its own login URL and is required for SSO. **Just-in-time provisioning** creates or updates a Salesforce user the first time they log in through SSO. For customers, Experience Cloud supports social sign-on and self-registration.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce System Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Because the credential is made up of four exams, prepare for each one separately. These are the themes that show up across them.

blocks.heading: Enterprise Integration Patterns
blocks.body: If the user waits, it is synchronous. If not, prefer asynchronous. If the data is huge, use Bulk API. If it shouldn't be copied, use Salesforce Connect.

blocks.heading: Data Migration Strategy
blocks.body: Load parent records before children, use external IDs to link them, turn off automation that isn't needed during the load, and use Bulk API for large volumes.

blocks.heading: Multi-Org Architecture
blocks.body: One org is simpler and is usually the default answer. Several orgs make sense for strict legal separation or very different business units, but they need integration between them.

blocks.heading: Governor Limits at Scale
blocks.body: Design for bulk from the start. Move callouts and heavy work to Queueable or Batch Apex, and keep queries selective on large objects.

blocks.heading: Salesforce Connect & External Objects
blocks.body: Use these when users need to see outside data that changes often and shouldn't be stored in Salesforce.

nextCertsAfter.heading: What to Do After System Architect
nextCertsAfter.intro: Once you hold System Architect and Application Architect, the next step is Technical Architect (CTA):

sampleQuestions.question: Which set of credentials earns you System Architect?
options: Platform Developer I plus the three architect exams
Administrator, Platform App Builder, Data Architect, Sharing and Visibility Architect
Administrator, Advanced Administrator, Platform Developer II
sampleQuestions.explanation: System Architect is granted when you hold these four credentials. There is no separate exam.
whyWrong: There is no stand-alone System Architect exam.
That list is close to the Application Architect requirements, not System Architect.
Those credentials don't make up any architect credential.

sampleQuestions.question: A partner's server needs to call the Salesforce API every hour with no person logging in. Which OAuth flow fits best?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The JWT bearer flow is meant for server-to-server access. The server signs a token with a certificate, and no password or user is needed.
whyWrong: The device flow is for devices with limited input, such as TVs; and still needs a person.
The web server flow needs a person to log in through a browser.
The user-agent flow is for browser or mobile apps with a user present.

sampleQuestions.question: Employees log in to many company apps with Okta. They should log in to Salesforce the same way. What roles do Okta and Salesforce play?
options: Salesforce is the identity provider and Okta the service provider instead
Okta is the identity provider and Salesforce is the service provider
Neither, because this needs OAuth only
sampleQuestions.explanation: The system that checks the user's identity is the identity provider, here Okta. The app the user logs in to is the service provider, here Salesforce.
whyWrong: Only one system authenticates the user in this setup.
That reverses the roles. Okta is checking the login, not Salesforce.
SSO for employees is usually SAML. OAuth is about granting apps access to data.

sampleQuestions.question: When a new employee logs in to Salesforce through SSO for the first time, a user account should be created for them automatically. What feature does this?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Just-in-time provisioning uses details in the SAML assertion to create or update the Salesforce user during their first SSO login.
whyWrong: Login flows add steps after login, such as a terms page. They are not built for creating users.
Delegated authentication checks a password against another system. It doesn't create users.
Permission set groups grant access to existing users.

sampleQuestions.question: A company must load 3 million Contacts linked to 400,000 Accounts from an old CRM. What is the right approach?
options: Use the REST API one record at a time
Enter the records by hand in batches
Load Accounts with external IDs, then Contacts
sampleQuestions.explanation: Parents must exist before children. External IDs let you link Contacts to Accounts without looking up Salesforce IDs, and Bulk API handles the volume.
whyWrong: Millions of single REST calls would be slow and hit API limits.
Manual entry is impossible at this scale.
Contacts can't link to Accounts that don't exist yet.

sampleQuestions.question: Two business units have very different processes, and a regulator requires their customer data to be kept fully separate. What org strategy fits?
options: One org with different record types
One org with different apps in the App Launcher
One org with different page layouts
Separate orgs for each business unit
sampleQuestions.explanation: Strict legal separation is one of the few strong reasons for multiple orgs. Record types and apps don't separate the data itself.
whyWrong: Record types change processes but keep data in the same org.
Apps change navigation, not who can reach the data.
Page layouts only change how records look.

sampleQuestions.question: What is required before you can set up SAML single sign-on for a Salesforce org?
sampleQuestions.explanation: My Domain gives the org its own login URL, which SSO needs. It is turned on for all orgs today.
whyWrong: Encryption is not needed for SSO.
Experience Cloud is for external sites. Employee SSO doesn't need it.
SSO can be set up in any org. A Full sandbox is for testing.

sampleQuestions.question: Order data from a warehouse system must be visible to service agents in Salesforce. It changes every few minutes and must not be stored in Salesforce. What fits?
options: A custom object that is updated once every hour
sampleQuestions.explanation: Salesforce Connect reads the data live from the other system each time it is viewed. Nothing is copied into Salesforce.
whyWrong: An hourly copy stores the data and can be an hour old.
A nightly load copies the data and is up to a day old.
Outbound messages send data out of Salesforce, not in.

sampleQuestions.question: A trigger needs to send each new Order to an ERP. Calls to the ERP take several seconds. What is the best design?
options: Have the trigger queue Apex for the callout
Ask users to click a button to send each Order
A synchronous callout in the trigger
A nightly batch job that sends the orders
sampleQuestions.explanation: Triggers can't make synchronous callouts. Queueable Apex runs the callout in the background and can be chained or retried.
whyWrong: A manual button depends on people remembering to click it.
Triggers aren't allowed to make synchronous callouts, and the user would wait.
A nightly job delays every Order by up to a day, which may be too late.

sampleQuestions.question: Five systems need customer data from SAP. Today each one has its own direct connection to SAP, and every change breaks something. What should the architect recommend?
options: Copy SAP data into every system each night
sampleQuestions.explanation: A single System API in front of SAP, reused by everyone; means only one connection to change when SAP changes.
whyWrong: Another direct link adds to the mess.
Nightly copies are stale and still need five integrations.
The business still needs the data.

sampleQuestions.question: Code is being deployed to production. What test coverage rule applies to Apex?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Production deployments that include Apex need at least 75% overall coverage, and every trigger must be covered.
whyWrong: All Apex in production needs coverage, not just packages.
Tests are required for Apex in production.
100% is a goal, not the rule.

sampleQuestions.question: The release team wants to check that a deployment will pass in production on Monday, then deploy it fast during a short window on Wednesday. What should they use?
options: A change set uploaded on Wednesday
Deploy on Monday and roll back if needed
sampleQuestions.explanation: A validated deployment can be quick deployed within 10 days without running tests again.
whyWrong: A new change set on Wednesday would run tests during the short window.
There is no rollback button in Salesforce.
Running all tests makes the window longer, not shorter.

sampleQuestions.question: A mobile app used by customers needs to call Salesforce on behalf of the logged-in customer and keep them logged in for weeks. What should be used?
options: An API key in the app
An OAuth flow with a refresh token
A shared integration user for all customers
sampleQuestions.explanation: A refresh token lets the app get new access tokens without asking the user to log in again, and access stays tied to that customer.
whyWrong: Salesforce doesn't use API keys this way, and a key in an app can be extracted.
The username and password flow stores real passwords and is not recommended.
A shared user loses the link between actions and the real customer.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should an Apex callout get the endpoint URL and login details for an outside system?
options: A text field on a custom object
sampleQuestions.explanation: Named Credentials store the URL and authentication securely, and Salesforce adds the login details to each call for you.
whyWrong: Custom Labels are for translations, not secrets.
A text field exposes the secret to anyone who can read the record.
Hard-coded secrets can be read by anyone with code access and need a deployment to change.

sampleQuestions.question: Which tool should a team use as the source of truth for their org's metadata?
options: A version control system like Git
sampleQuestions.explanation: In source-driven development, Git holds the real version of the metadata. Orgs are built and updated from it.
whyWrong: Sandboxes get refreshed and lose work.
Production changes all the time and has no history of who changed what.
A spreadsheet isn't the metadata and quickly goes out of date.
